html:
The Sumerian city-states were the first cities and states in the world, built by the Sumerians in southern Mesopotamia, today's southern Iraq, from about 3300 BCE until Sargon of Akkad conquered them around 2334 BCE.

Farmers here dug canals from the Tigris and Euphrates to water fields of barley in a land with almost no rain. The surplus fed cities. Uruk grew into the largest city of its time, and others followed: Ur, Lagash, Umma, Kish, Nippur and Eridu.

  • Each city had its own god, whose temple owned land, herds and workshops. Later a king, or lugal, ruled beside the temple.
  • To keep track of grain, sheep and workers, scribes at Uruk invented writing around 3200 BCE. It grew into cuneiform.
  • Temples stood on stepped platforms that later grew into ziggurats such as the Ziggurat of Ur.
  • They also gave us the wheel for carts, counting in sixties (still used for minutes and degrees) and the first known literature.

The cities were rarely united. They fought each other for water and land; the border war between Lagash and Umma lasted generations. Around 2334 BCE Sargon, a Semitic-speaking king, took them all and founded the Akkadian Empire. Sumerian rule came back briefly under Ur III, but after 2000 BCE Sumerian died out as a spoken language. Scribes kept it alive as a learned language for nearly two thousand years, the way Latin was kept in medieval Europe, and the stories of kings like Gilgamesh lived on in the Epic of Gilgamesh.
sum: The Sumerian city-states were the first cities and states in the world, built by the Sumerians in southern Mesopotamia, today's southern Iraq, from about 3300 BCE until Sargon of Akkad conquered them around 2334 BCE.
